value.overview: The Common Black Hawk (Buteogallus anthracinus) is a broad-winged raptor associated with rivers, wetlands, mangroves, and other warm lowland habitats. Adults are mostly black or dark charcoal, with a broad white band and white tip on the short tail, yellow legs, and a yellow-based bill. Juveniles are brown and heavily streaked. Despite its name, it is not closely related to the Zone-tailed Hawk and is generally more strongly tied to aquatic habitats.
value.classification: The Common Black Hawk belongs to the order Accipitriformes and the hawk and eagle family Accipitridae. Its genus, Buteogallus, includes several large tropical black hawks.
value.identification: Adults are nearly uniform black or dark gray, with broad wings, a short tail, yellow legs, and yellow skin at the base of the bill. A single broad white tail band and a white tail tip are conspicuous in flight. The underwing may appear somewhat paler than the body. Juveniles are brown above and pale below, with dark streaking, a dark facial stripe, and a more barred tail. It can be confused with the larger Great Black Hawk, which usually has more extensive white in the tail and wings.
value.rangeHabitat: The species ranges from the southwestern United States and Mexico through Central America to northern South America, with additional populations in the Caribbean. In Costa Rica it is a resident species, locally common along both the Pacific and Caribbean coasts but uncommon or scarce inland. It uses mangrove swamps, estuaries, coastal woodland, river margins, wet lowland forest, and dry woodland near water. Large rivers can allow it to occur farther inland where suitable prey and nesting trees remain available.
value.migrationStatus: Costa Rican populations are generally resident and do not undertake regular long-distance migration. The migratory portion of the species occurs mainly in the northern range, especially the southwestern United States and parts of northwestern Mexico; those birds move south in the nonbreeding season and may pass through or winter farther south.
value.breeding: Breeding occurs in suitable lowland habitats, especially near rivers, estuaries, mangroves, and other wetlands. The nest is a bulky platform of sticks placed in a tree, often near water, and may be reused or repaired in later years. The female usually lays a small clutch, commonly one or two eggs. Both adults defend the nesting area, and the young remain dependent on the parents for an extended period after leaving the nest.
value.dietFeeding: Its diet varies with location and season. Common prey includes crabs, crayfish, fish, frogs, snakes, lizards, small mammals, and large insects. In coastal Central America, land crabs and other aquatic or shoreline animals can be especially important. The hawk often hunts from a low or exposed perch beside water, dropping to the ground or water's edge to seize prey, and may also search slowly along mudflats and mangrove margins.
value.behavior: Common Black Hawks are often seen perched quietly in trees beside water or soaring on broad wings over wetlands and forest edges. They are generally less constantly active than many smaller hawks, but may make short flights between perches while hunting. Adults are territorial during breeding. Their calls are high, clear, and repeated, especially around the nest. They may tolerate some human-modified landscapes when riverside trees, wetlands, and adequate prey are retained.

conservation.populationTrend: The recognized population trend is decreasing.
